en: Wondrously beautiful, with narrow eyes,
Someone accompanied him.
Seen from the front,
He had the awe of six thousand warriors;
Seen from behind,
He had the appearance of a dragon.
His face was like oiled wheat,
His eyes like mist at dusk;
His right shoulder was broad.
Whenever his fury seized him,
The eighteen thousand worlds
He was a warrior who could lay waste.
His brow was high, his wrath was fierce,
He lays flat whoever attacks him.
Konurbay, khan of Beijing,
Would flee without facing him;
If he faced Manas's heroic son,
He would fall dead.
If Toltoy and Kojo
Charged in with spears and cries,
He would throw them into turmoil.
Broad-chested and wide-breasted,
He was a majestic lion;
Among the giants upon the earth,
He was a warrior fit to stand alone.
Never turning back before death,
This gray wolf, let alone Toltoy,
Would not retreat even from hell.
No one could come against him;
Whoever faced him would die.
Tall and broad-shouldered,
Both champion and lion,
She had found the man destined for her
And stood there amazed.
He was an exceptionally born lion,
Tiger-hearted and thick-necked;
Fortunate Semetey
Was a red fortress of iron
Established for these Kyrgyz.
Standing proud and taking none as his equal,
Refusing to count any man his peer—
Such conduct suited the gray wolf.
That she had sought so long without finding him
Was a God-stricken affair.
Could there be a man who would not join
In true amusement and delight,
Who would not lie playfully pinching
And teasing the gray wolf?”
Aychürök rejoiced greatly;
Sitting and looking sidelong,
Filling her gaze with his bearing,
She sat looking at him imploringly,
Filling her heart with him.
The mount beneath him,
The peerless courser Narbuudan—
If you look to his origins,
He was kin to Kyz Saykal's Algara.
He was born of the same stock as that horse.
Manas had taken a liking to him as a foal,
When he was brought as a gift.
“Someone may cast the evil eye,” he said,
And had an owl plume fastened to his head;
He had him raised in a dark place,
And many judges of horses admired him.
He curved his neck like a stag;
When game appeared within bowshot,
He sprang without hesitation.
Gold ornament was laid on him by the foot,
And khans who saw him asked for him.
He was not given to those who asked;
Far from being given away, not even
A ritually unwashed person had ridden Buurul.
He was a horse raised with honor;
Anyone who slighted him became an outsider.
Narbuudan stood apart;
The White Falcon was on his arm,
And the White Hound followed him.
Semetey, son of Manas,
Loomed like Opol-Too;
Wherever Chürök saw him,
Her heart broke away from her:
“His eyes are like the depths of a lake;
If Konurbay came openly,
He could swallow him with all his countless host.
If Chynkojo, son of Shygay,
Came to contest him, he could slaughter him;
Toltoy, son of Bagysh,
He could leave utterly destroyed.
I flew over Uch-Tum, Beijing and Bakburchun;
I saw the great men of those peoples.
Ever since then I have wandered,
Unable to find such a renowned man,
Unable to find such a lion among mortals,
I have merely been braiding
The dear hair grown down my back;
Unable to test and take my destined man,
I have only been living toward death.
His fortunes were complete;
He was a lion supported by the spirits.
My wandering to Temirkhan's city
Was evidently fitting.
A golden skullcap upon her head,
Unable to find her bearings,
The wretched daughter of Akun!
Her white throat gleamed,
Her fair face shone;
Sixty clasps and forty pearl buttons
Rattled upon her breast.
Look at the sweetness of your sister-in-law
Who went in search of a man; hear her words,
Look at her camel-calf eyes,
Her waist a handful wide, her face like the moon—
Your famous sister-in-law, the wretched one.
Deeply distressed, unable to rest,
She stood looking at the hero.
Unable to approach him openly,
Chürök's mind was divided:
If she seized him with entreaties,
Her ill-mannered kinsman, alas,
Seemed likely to use force.
If he caught her on the steppe, leaving her shamed,
Saying, “My wife came to me herself,”
And refused to go, provoking a quarrel,
Would Toltoy of the Jediger
Raid my father Akun
And destroy us all together?
If I went and married him myself,
I would mount the horse of disgrace
And earn a bad name.
In anguish she gave a harsh cry;
A great golden earring
Rattled upon her breast.
The famed beauty, her face like the moon,
Could make desire descend upon anyone who looked;
The radiant wretched woman
Had, above her lips,
A slightly protruding feature,
That Chürök who sought a husband.
Where was any defect
In your exhausted, unfortunate sister-in-law?
There are two versions of her fate;
Of noble, unfortunate Chürök
There are two different accounts.
Some people say,
“Chürök is Akun's daughter,”
And some people say,
“Chürök is the hero's daughter;
Without marrying until she grew old,
She brought turmoil upon her people.”
Thus Aychürök,
Finding no man to marry,
Finding no place to settle,
Searched the whole world,
Roamed through all the universe,
Flying about in her search,
And saw him while still captivated.
Let us leave this matter here
And begin from another side.
Two companions were beside him:
One was his tiger worth a thousand men,
The spring flowing down from the ridge,
The lamp left as a gift
By the hero Almambet—
Almambet's son Külchoro.
There was no such youth in the world;
This filthy world creates
Its servants in every kind of form.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Was a blazing red ember.
If all the eighteen thousand worlds
Were gathered together entire,
There would be no youth like him;
He was a flaming red arrow.
She marveled as she looked:
Almighty God creates
People in every different way.
The horse he rode was bay;
Unless Semetey's fortune was greater,
He was a man a full fathom tall.
Kanchoro, son of Chubak,
Was a black-hearted man;
And Tölöbay, son of Tölök,
Was a man who could make
A band of Jediger cry out in distress.
That I flew away without testing them
Was a God-stricken affair.”
Unable to find her bearings,
Your sister-in-law was sorely troubled.
She could neither follow behind him,
Nor go openly and marry him;
Your unfortunate Chürök was a marvel,
The poor woman kept changing form.
Semetey, son of the gray wolf,
Circled around Kötörmö;
He had seven bustards and six geese
Taken and bound together.
He made Buurul surge beneath him,
Made him strain as though his master had died;
He loomed like Opol-Too.
Each time Chürök saw him,
Her heart was painfully divided,
And she stood watching from concealment.
From the fortress with its gates,
From Chachykey's encampment,
The pampered wife Chachykey,
Wrapped in a lynx-fur coat,
Prepared to speak fondly
As she came before Semetey:
“You say you will fly the falcon each day,
And leave me burning with worry;
You linger long upon the steppe
And bring me this suffering.
Though I am here, you say you will fly the falcon
And cast me into distress;
You go far out upon the steppe,
Where there are many pale, broken mountains,
And many enemies ready to grapple with you.
There are Chinese along the frontier;
You have many deeds to perform.
A gun is before you,
And many enemies await a contest.
The Kyrgyz migrate through Talas;
Many people there bear grudges against you.
The Kyrgyz migrate through Keng-Kol;
Everyone you meet bears a grudge against you.
Month after month, saying you will fly your falcon,
You go away into the steppe,
Leaving me staring like a fool
And placing me in misery.”
Chachykey spoke fondly in this way
And walked directly toward him;
She became exceedingly affectionate.
Semey the hero, son of Manas,
That learned man who had studied scripture, said:
“We flew the falcon and surveyed the land;
It thoroughly inspected the watchposts.
We had seven bustards and six geese
Taken for us,
“Senior wife, we have brought them as a gift.”
So he said,
Then he put his hands behind his back,
That dear, immovable hero.
That dear, immovable lion,
When alone with his wife,
Was utterly overcome.
That dear lion, tender toward women,
Climbed down from his horse with a ringing sound.
When her lord dismounted,
His knee bent to the ground;
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Ran as swiftly as an arrow
And reached the weary Buurul,
Taking hold of him.
At the cast-iron-rooted copper post,
He tied the wretched man's Buurul
With an especially firm tether.
